newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN DLR REBUFFED IN ATTEMPT TO TAKE US$0.74.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN DLR REBUFFED IN ATTEMPT TO TAKE US$0.74.

text.p: The Australian dollar reached its highest level in a week as it built on overnight gains in Tuesday morning trade, but found itself rebuffed on attempts to break above US$0.7400.
The dollar traded a high of US$0.7405, its first time above US$0.7400 since last Tuesday, but ran into selling that saw it fall towards its lows for the morning at just above US$0.7380.
By noon (0200 GMT) the dollar was trading at US$0.7389/94, an improvement on its early US$0.7383/88 and comfortably above Monday's local close of US$0.7362/67.
Traders said some shortcovering and local buying after the Australian dollar's gains totalling three quarters of a cent in the last two offshore sessions had seen the dollar edge higher.
"There are rumours of some large amounts being bought and sold...there were a number of stop losses up higher and people were aware of those this morning," one trader said.
While the dollar remained under US$0.74, demand was able to soak up the selling interest, which traders said was mainly from Asian players.
But the sell orders above US$0.74 swamped the buyers and sent the dollar back towards support.
The unit held its overnight gains on the crosses, matching the U.S. dollar's performance in morning trade of being slightly lower against the yen and slightly better against the mark.
The Australian dollar was at 85.56/66 yen and 1.3764/76 marks from an early 85.74/84 and 1.3754/67 and a local close on Monday of 84.72/82 and 1.3588/3605.
In trade weighted terms the dollar held steady at 58.1 through the morning after rising overnight from a 57.6 close.
News of a 0.2 percent rise in June manufacturing output prices had little impact on the market, which has become used to data showing little evidence of inflationary pressures.
In a very quiet week for data, traders are waiting on a speech by the Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane later today in the hope it provides some leads.

Macfarlane will talk on the topic of monetary policy and growth in his first appearance since the July 30 rate cut and the early July announcement that the RBA had sold two thirds of its gold reserves earlier this year.
Macfarlane will be the after dinner speaker at a function in Perth, which because of time differences means he will not start talking until about 11.00 p.m. Sydney time, or 1300 GMT.
